understanding.core_idea: Paging replaces a process's contiguous memory requirement with fixed-size frames, at the cost of an extra address-translation step and some internal fragmentation.
key_points: the last page is rarely full

teaching_sequence.purpose: Establish why a single unbroken block causes external fragmentation
teaching_sequence.explanation_goal: Learner understands the problem paging is solving

teaching_sequence.purpose: Show memory split into fixed-size units that need not be adjacent

teaching_sequence.concept: The page table translates every access
teaching_sequence.purpose: Explain the mechanism that makes scattered frames usable
teaching_sequence.explanation_goal: Learner understands the cost paging adds in exchange

concrete_examples: A 4.5KB process on 4KB pages needs 2 frames, and the second is half-empty.

example_plan.example: A 4.5KB process on 4KB pages needs 2 frames, and the second is half-empty.

common_confusions: Learners assume paging has no cost because it removes external fragmentation, missing the translation overhead and internal fragmentation it introduces.

confusion_plan.confusion: Paging is not free: it trades one waste (external fragmentation) for two costs (a translation step, and internal fragmentation on the last page).

source_evidence: The average waste is half a page per process, which is why very large page sizes are not automatically better.
